newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Guarded market response to RBNZ cash rate plan.
newsitem.headline: Guarded market response to RBNZ cash rate plan.

text.p: Analysts gave a less than enthusiastic welcome on Friday to a suggestion by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand that it might adopt an official cash rate range as the key lever for monetary policy.

Unlike nearly every other central bank in the industrialised world, the RBNZ does not set rates administratively. Its current money market management operations rely purely on regulating the amount of cash in the system.
The bank argues in a discussion paper that a cash rate scheme similar to Canada's would provide a more reliable lever for keeping monetary conditions within the required broad range.
It suggests switching to an official cash rate range, reviewed each week, to replace the daily target for settlement cash balances.
However, some analysts spoken to by Reuters questioned the need to introduce a new system, arguing the old one was working well and just needed some fine tuning.
"They are very, very close to having an excellent system, if they just showed a bit of patience," National Bank economist Adrian Orr said.

He said the RBNZ had made clear its assumed trade-off between the currency's Trade-Weighted Index and short term interest rates. Since its last statement in December, markets had stuck very tightly to its desired monetary conditions.
"We know all the other coefficients, they provide us with their inflation forecasts and then they should just go home. What they are saying now is don't worry yourselves, we know best," Orr said.

Bancorp Executive Director Roger Kerr said he was not at all in favour of moving to an official rate band, and the Australian experience suggested some market participants heard about an impending change in the rate before others.
Kerr acknowledged there had been incidents in the past when the RBNZ's signalling methods had prompted over-reaction in the markets, but doubted a new system was the answer.
"I think there are probably weaknesses and room for improvement on both sides, but I'd rather look to improve that than move to having a set discount rate," Kerr said.

ANZ Bank Treasurer Grant Spencer said the proposed changes held potential to improve the efficiency of monetary policy operation, but it was important the RBNZ's settings should generally follow the market rather than led it.

"From time to time occasionally they'll want to lead the market, but...most of the time, if this is going to represent an improvement, then we want most weekly adjustments to be fairly ho-hum and predictable," he said.
The bank should beware of increasing market volatility, particularly in the exchange rate, added Spencer.
"If they started to make policy adjustments week to week and have the market on the edge of their seats every Wednesday at 9.30, then I'd say that would be a backward step."
He said ANZ would be making a formal submission to the RBNZ, which has invited views from the market.

Australia's Citibank senior economist Stephen Koukoulas said the changes would make an already transparent monetary policy system even more transparent, and brought it closer to that used in Australia.
"It avoids them having to intervene in cash every day and put in a few dollars in and a few dollars out to keep the system relatively stable," he said.

Economists agreed the new system would not allow the RBNZ to correct perceived imbalances between interest rates and the exchange rate. These would continue to be market-determined and the bank was powerless to change that.
The RBNZ has repeatedly said it would prefer higher interest rates and a lower currency.
